reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Narrowing of the airway at the subglottis, the region just below the vocal cords, which is the narrowest part of the paediatric airway and bounded by the complete cricoid ring
It may be congenital or acquired, and prolonged endotracheal intubation is the leading acquired cause
Presents with biphasic stridor, recurrent or prolonged croup-like episodes, exertional breathlessness, and in severe cases respiratory distress
In infants it can masquerade as recurrent croup or failure to extubate after ventilation
Endoscopic assessment of the airway defines the site, length, and severity of narrowing, and grading systems (such as Cotton-Myer) quantify the degree of luminal loss
Management depends on severity and ranges from observation and endoscopic dilatation or laser to open reconstruction such as laryngotracheal reconstruction or cricotracheal resection
A tracheostomy may be needed to secure the airway in severe or complex cases before or during definitive repair
Minimising intubation trauma and duration, and using appropriately sized tubes, helps prevent acquired stenosis
reference.pathophysiology: Subglottic stenosis is a fixed reduction in the cross-sectional area of the subglottic airway. The congenital form reflects abnormal development of the cricoid cartilage producing an inherently narrow lumen. The acquired form typically follows mucosal injury, most often from a tightly fitting or prolonged endotracheal tube, which causes pressure ischaemia, ulceration, perichondritis, and healing by fibrosis with scar contracture; trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, and prior airway surgery are other causes. Because the cricoid is a complete non-expansile ring, even modest circumferential scarring or oedema markedly reduces the lumen and airflow.
additionalDifferentials: Vascular ring or extrinsic tracheal compression
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting the airway
additionalInvestigations: Flexible and rigid endoscopy of the airway to assess and grade the stenosis
Sizing of the airway with endotracheal tubes to quantify the degree of narrowing
Cross-sectional imaging to map the length of the stenotic segment and exclude external compression
Evaluation for inflammatory or autoimmune disease when clinically suspected
Assessment of reflux, which can aggravate airway inflammation
redFlags: Progressive stridor with respiratory distress indicating critical airway narrowing requiring urgent airway control
Failure to extubate or recurrent severe respiratory episodes in an infant
Rapidly worsening obstruction suggesting superimposed oedema or infection on a fixed stenosis
Signs of an underlying systemic inflammatory disease driving the stenosis
reference.prognosis: Mild congenital stenosis often improves as the airway grows, and mild acquired disease may respond to endoscopic measures; more severe or long-segment stenosis usually needs open reconstruction, which has good success in restoring an adequate airway, though multiple procedures and temporary tracheostomy are sometimes required.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating a child for croup while missing a fixed subglottic stenosis
Using oversized endotracheal tubes and prolonging intubation, promoting acquired stenosis
Underestimating severity by relying on symptoms alone without endoscopic grading
Overlooking an inflammatory cause such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Observe mild congenital stenosis, which often improves as the airway grows
Endoscopic balloon dilatation, with laser scar division and adjunctive intralesional corticosteroid or mitomycin, for suitable short-segment disease
Open reconstruction by laryngotracheal reconstruction with cartilage grafting or cricotracheal resection for severe or long-segment stenosis
Tracheostomy to secure the airway in severe or acute obstruction
Treat aggravating gastro-oesophageal reflux with acid suppression and control airway inflammation
Institute immunosuppression where an underlying inflammatory or autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis is identified
Manage within a specialist airway multidisciplinary team, anticipating that staged or repeated procedures may be needed
